extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and proofreaders preparing scholarly/press publications (University of Chicago Press style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for punctuation, hyphenation, word divisions, and footnote conventions for preparing manuscripts for publication; aimed at ensuring consistent copyedited text according to University of Chicago Press practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 159. Comma after thousands
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except in a date or in a page-reference; and not between the constituents of dimensions, weights, and measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; but 2200 B.C.; p. 2461; measures: 3 feet 6 inches; 4 lb. 2 oz.; 2 hr. 4 min. Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma with four figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 160. Comma between month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year, and similar time divisions, by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906. Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma between month and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: 161. Omit comma in signatures and headers
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma, in signatures and at the beginning of articles, after author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 65 for cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 162. Comma placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following the parenthesis, if the context requires it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put comma inside "..."; when a parenthesis follows the quoted material, place comma after the parenthesis if context requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: 163. Apostrophe for contractions and omitted figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number. In contractions containing a verb and the negative, do not use a space between the two components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: it's, ne'er, 'twas, 'takin' me 'at'; m'f'g; the class of '96; don't, haven't. See also rule 123.

rubrics_metrics.name: 164. Forming possessive case with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s (see rule 113).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word; horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Jones's farms; Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: 165. Apostrophe in plurals of numerals and rare coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, by adding an apostrophe alone (mono-syllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others, s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the i poo's; in two's and three's; the three R's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; "these I-just-do-as-I-please's"; "all the Tommy Atkins' of England" (but: the Rosses and the Macdougals); the Pericles' and Socrates' of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks cross-reference
rubrics_metrics.description: See the section on Quotations (74-91) for rules governing quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 166. Use of dash for sudden break or emphatic pause
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash is used to denote 'a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative quotations show dramatic pauses: "Do we — can we — send out... ?"; "To be or not to be — that is the question".

rubrics_metrics.name: 167. Dashes for parenthetical clauses that are independent interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This may be said to be — but, never mind, we will pass over that"; when the parenthetical is structurally independent, prefer dashes (see 150).

rubrics_metrics.name: 168. Dash to introduce emphasis or expanded clause that repeats phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas"; "Here we are face to face with a new and difficult problem — new and difficult, that is, in the sense that..."

rubrics_metrics.name: 169. Use dash when 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons..."

rubrics_metrics.name: 170. Dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final—summarizing—clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Amos, with the idea that Jehovah is an upright judge...; Hosea, whose Master hated injustice...; Isaiah, whose Lord would have mercy... — these were the spokesmen..."

rubrics_metrics.name: 171. Dash after a word/phrase set on its own line followed by paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example layout: "I recommend — i. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him."

rubrics_metrics.name: 172. Dash for side-heads/run-in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "2. The language of the New Testament. — The lexicons of Grimm-Thayer..." Also used for run-in side-heads and par. heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: 173. Dash in place of 'to' and en/em dash distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers (see 158). Use en dash for spans like May–July, em dash for larger separations and for clause breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em dash); pp. 3–7 (en dash). But if 'from' precedes the first word/number, do not use dash instead of 'to' (write 'From May 1 to July 1, 1906'). Rules for connecting consecutive numbers: omit hundreds from second number unless first ends in two ciphers; B.C. dates repeat hundreds: 1880–95, pp. 113–16; 1900–1906, pp. 102–7; 387–324 B.C. Note: Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette repeat hundreds (1880–1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: 174. Dash before reference following a complete-sentence quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation, consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I felt an emotion of the moral sublime...' — Thirty Years, I, 379. Also used in placing author/title after a poem excerpt: —Emerson, "To Ellen, at the South."

rubrics_metrics.name: 175. Avoid using dash with other punctuation except period; comma may be retained before dash in special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period. But if a comma would be necessary without the parenthetical set off by dashes, the comma may be retained before the first dash; when the parenthetical requires an interrogation or exclamation, that punctuation may be retained with the second dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: "DEAR SIR:— I have..." Correct: "DEAR SIR: I have..." Example of retaining comma: "Darwin, the promulgator of the theory, — though by no means its only supporter — is regarded today..." Example of retaining ? or !: "Senator Blank — shall we call him statesman or politician? — introduced the bill."

rubrics_metrics.name: 176. Parentheses for enumerative figures/letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example inline enumeration: "The reasons... were three: (i) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel." If paragraphed, single parenthesis with lower-case italic letter; period with figures and capital letters. Syllabi use a specific indention/notation scheme (A., I., 1., a), (1), (a), i), ii) ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: 177. Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise from less distinctive marks, or unless the content is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use dashes when clause is integrated or editorial; parentheses permitted for aside remarks or references: "The period thus inaugurated (of which I shall speak at greater length...) was characterized by..." (see 150 & 167).

rubrics_metrics.name: 178. Uses of brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for each use are provided: editorial note in brackets, interpolation in quoted material, correction of name spelling using [s], bibliographic supply, and nested citations such as references in brackets for editions/pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 179. Brackets for 'To be continued' markers, table-of-contents usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'To be continued' at the end, and 'Continued from...' at the beginning of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics, and reduced in type size per reduction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] [To be concluded]

rubrics_metrics.name: 180. Ellipses to indicate omission or lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in quoted documents; for ellipsis at beginning/middle/end of a sentence, four periods separated by a space (en quad) should ordinarily be used (except in very narrow measures). If preceding line ends in a point, omit that in the four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When whole paragraph(s) or complete poetic lines are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length; periods should not extend beyond the longest type-line. Examples provided in prose and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: 181. Treat ellipsis as part of citation and enclose in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as a part of the citation; consequently should be inclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 178(3) for quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 182. Hyphenation at line breaks and between compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line and between many compound words. Modern tendency is against hyphen; many compound words better written as single two words which convey one idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of consolidated forms: schoolroom, workshop, headquarters. Guidance: rules follow but require judgment; not rigidly applied in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 183. Hyphenate multiword adjectives before nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun, or when the noun is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus; well-known author; first-class investment; better-trained teachers; high-school course; half-dead horse; up-to-date machinery; four-year-old boy. Do not connect adjectives with adverbs ending in -ly; when following the noun, or qualifying a predicate, hyphen not required. Where one component contains more than one word, use en dash: New York–Chicago freight traffic. Exceptions: New Testament times, Old English spelling, a priori argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: 184. Hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, fool-killer, office-holder, well-wisher, property-owner; hero-worship, child-study; wood-turning, clay-modeling. Exceptions: common/unwieldy compounds like lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader.

rubrics_metrics.name: 185. Hyphenate certain present-participle+noun formations
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united (i) with a noun to form a new noun with a meaning different from the two words separately, or (2) with a preposition used absolutely to form a noun, may properly take a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, dwelling-place, printing-office, walking-stick, starting-point, stepping-stone, stumbling-block.

rubrics_metrics.name: 186. Rule for compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, compounds of book, house, mill, room, shop, and work: when prefixed noun is one syllable, print as one word; when two syllables, hyphenate; when three or more, print as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook; pocket-book, story-book; boathouse, clubhouse; engine-house, power-house; cornmill, water-mill; bedroom, classroom; tinshop, workshop; exceptions and rare combinations noted (source-book, wheat-mill, school work).

rubrics_metrics.name: 187. Hyphenate occupation compound words and adjectival nouns before proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of maker, dealer, and other occupation words should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns combined in an adjectival sense before a proper noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman; poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions: bookmaker, dressmaker, shopgirl.

rubrics_metrics.name: 188. Hyphenation for 'store' compounds depends on syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: 189. Hyphenate compounds of 'fellow' when first element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings; but playfellow; exceptions: 'Mr. Goodfellow'; phrase politics makes strange bedfellows.

rubrics_metrics.name: 190. Hyphenate kinship compounds when first element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of father, mother, brother, sister, daughter, parent, and foster should be hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, sister-nation, foster-son, daughter-cells, parent-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: 191. Hyphenate 'great' in generational compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great', indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: 192. Hyphenate compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: 193. Compounds of 'skin' printing rules by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with words of one syllable are printed as one word; with words of more than one, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 194. Hyphenate compounds of 'master'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: 195. Hyphenate compounds when 'god' is second element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'god', when this word forms the second element of the compound, should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god (but: godsend, godson).

rubrics_metrics.name: 196. Hyphen after 'half', 'quarter', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half', 'quarter', etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, half-year, half-title, quarter-mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: 197. Use of hyphen with prefixes semi-, demi-, bi-, tri-
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-, demi-, bi-, tri-, etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen unless followed by i, w, or y; exceptions for long or unusual formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, bipartisan, bichromate, trimonthly, tricolor; but semi-barbarous, semi-translucent. Also bi-weekly, tri-yearly when readability required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 198. Hyphenate compounds beginning with 'self-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'self', when this word forms the first element of the compound, are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 199. Compounds with 'fold' printed as one word or two by syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are printed as one word if the number contains only one syllable; if more, as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: 200. Adjectives formed with suffix 'like' rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun are usually printed as one word if the noun contains only one syllable (except when ending in l); if it contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, warlike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, business-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: 201. Hyphenate parts of titles like 'vice-', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', 'lieutenant'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vice', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', and 'lieutenant', constituting parts of titles, should be connected with the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 202. Hyphenate 'by-' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'by-', when this word forms the first element of the compound, should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws (but: bygones).

rubrics_metrics.name: 203. Hyphenation of co-, pre-, re- with like vowel or w/y
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', and 're-', when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, or by w or y, take a hyphen; as a rule they do not when followed by a different vowel or a consonant, except to avoid mispronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter, co-worker, re-yield; but coequal, coeducation, prearranged, reinstal. Note Botanical Gazette prints: cooperate, reenter. Exceptions include proper names, long/unusual formations, and words where omission would change meaning: pre-Raphaelite, re-democratize, re-cover (=cover again), re-creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 204. Omit hyphen from today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint/standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen from 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'viewpoint', 'standpoint'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 119 cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 205. Negative particles un-, in-, il-, im-, a- usually no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-', 'in-', 'il-', 'im-', and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, indeterminate, illimitable, impersonal, asymmetrical. Exceptions are rare and artificial combinations. The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in common words: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious; but nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonplus, nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: 206. 'Quasi-' requires a hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi-' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 207. Over- and under- generally not hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in unusual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, underestimate, undersecretary; but: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: 208. Latin/Greek prepositional prefixes usually not hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin prepositions (ante, infra, inter, intra, post, sub, super, supra) and Greek 'anti' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen, unless followed by the letter with which they terminate, or, for vowel-ending prefixes, by w, y, or a vowel forming a diphthong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antediluvian, inframarginal, international, interstate, postscript, postgraduate, subconscious, submarine. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university, post-revolutionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 209. Extra-, pan-, ultra- usually take hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra', 'pan', and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, pan-Hellenic, ultra-conservative (but: extraordinary, Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: 210. Hyphenate fractional numbers spelled out between numerator and denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the year is two-thirds gone; four and five-sevenths; thirty one-hundredths; but: thirty-one hundredths. Avoid hyphenation in constructions like 'One half of his fortune...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 211. Hyphen indicate omitted common element in series of compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have a component in common, omit it from all but the last word and indicate the implication by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English- and Spanish-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces; quoted example: 'fifth- and tenth-century Europe' (some regard this hyphen objectionable).

rubrics_metrics.name: 212. Hyphen to indicate incomplete prefix or suffix
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The Spanish diminutive suffixes -ito and -cita.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 213. Hyphen to indicate syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 214. List of everyday words to be hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of common everyday words which should be hyphenated and do not fall under previous classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, anti-trust, death-rate, mid-year, subject-matter, bas-relief, first-fruits, nature-study, thought-process, birth-rate, folk-song, object-lesson, title-page, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 215. Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words. Wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference to keep words intact unless spacing forces division.

rubrics_metrics.name: 216. Do not divide on two-letter syllables in wide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, in wide measures (20 ems or more), divide on a syllable of two letters, if possible; never carry over a syllable of two letters. Words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid dividing 'only' as on-ly; words like oc-cur, of-fice, let-ter rarely divided. Good spacing is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: 217. Limit consecutive hyphenated line breaks and avoid division near paragraph end
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen if avoidable. The next to the last line in a paragraph ought not to end in a divided word; the last line ('breakline') in measures of 15 ems and up should contain at least four letters. Avoid divided word at bottom of right-hand page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layout considerations to improve readability and aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: 218. Do not divide proper nouns unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve integrity of names across line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 219. Do not separate initials or abbreviations across lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not separate (put in different lines) the initials of a name, or such combinations as A.D., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep initials and common abbreviations intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: 220. Avoid separation of divisional marks from the section they precede
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) in the middle of a sentence from the section which it precedes; do not allow such mark to fall at the end of a line, but carry it over with the matter to which it pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep enumeration markers attached to following text for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 221. Divide according to American pronunciation, not derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide according to pronunciation (the American system), not according to derivation (the English system). As far as compatible with pronunciation and good spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines or according to derivation and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); knowledge as knowl-edge; dis-pleasure preferable to displeas-ure. Avoid monstrosities like Passo-ver, diso-bedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: 222. Division between two consonants between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels, and the syllable ends on one consonant, the division may be made between the consonants, pronunciation determining place of division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, financier, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: 223. Do not terminate a line with soft c/g or j; avoid division
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or g, or in a j. Escape division entirely if possible; if not, divide at safer point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred divisions: pro-cess (not proc-ess); necessary: ne-cessary (not nec-essary); spacing: spacing not spac-ing. Note: this differs from some dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 224. Divide on a vowel where practicable; vowels alone in middle run into first line
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. If a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel into the next line (read-able not reada-ble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); particu-lar (not partic-ular); critique of exceptions for -able / -ible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 225. Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid additional hyphens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson (not object-les-son); fellow-being (not fel-low-being); poverty-stricken (not pov-erty-stricken).

rubrics_metrics.name: 226. Treat diphthongs as single letters in division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; therefore do not divide such sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not divide: people, Caesar, building.

rubrics_metrics.name: 227. Carry t into next line in derivatives when accent shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in t, the t in divisions should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative has retained the accent of the parent-word, the t should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect'); but: respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: 228. Addition of plural s does not justify dividing words ending in s-sound
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s, adding a new syllable to words ending in an s-sound, does not create a new excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: horse s and circumstan-ces are impossible divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 229. Adjectives in -ical divided on the i
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i: physi-cal, not phys-ical nor physic-al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place division to reflect correct syllable boundary and avoid misdivision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 230. Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple prohibition; maintain 'nothing' intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: 231. Condensed rules for dividing foreign-language words
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensed rules for dividing words in frequently encountered foreign languages (French, German, Italian, Spanish, Greek, Latin) are provided, covering syllabification and consonant-vowel division principles specific to each language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes multiple subrules per language: e.g., French divide on a vowel where possible; carry certain consonants; count syllables as vowels. German: divide on vowel; when several consonants between vowels carry last consonant over; certain clusters never separated (sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th). Italian/Spanish/Greek/Latin have analogous language-specific rules; see page for many examples. Use these when proofreading foreign terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 232. Use superior figures for reference indexes in text
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indexes, as a rule, use superior figures. Only in special cases should asterisks, daggers, etc., be employed (e.g., in tables or algebraic matter). Index figures in the text should be placed after the punctuation marks, without space, except in German where they are placed inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the niceties of style which were then invading Attic prose,1 and which made... Footnote 1 example: In particular the avoidance of hiatus. Use *, †, ‡, §, ||, ¶ sequence when figures are not used (see rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: 233. Use 'ibid.' for consecutive references; limit ibid. usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use ibid. instead of repeating the title. Ibid. takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ibid. should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso page; better to repeat the title if short, or use loc. cit. or op. cit. for other contexts. Examples of sequence: Spencer, Principles of Sociology, chap. iv. 3 Ibid., chap. v. 2 Ibid. 4 Spencer, loc. cit.

rubrics_metrics.name: 234. Footnotes to tables: size and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether the tables are ruled or open, should be in 6-pt, and should invariably be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page. For reference indexes in such cases use asterisks, etc., and not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table-specific footnote conventions: small type size (6-pt) and placement immediately below table; use symbols rather than superior figures for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 235. Omit author's name in footnote if given in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to, or a quotation from, his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: "I cannot admit ... ." Footnote: 1 Laws of the Ancients, I, 153. (Do not repeat Herbert in the footnote if named in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 236. Place index figure at end of quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to earlier illustration and preference for placing footnote markers after closing punctuation of quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 237. Abbreviation usage in references: omit Vol., chap., p. unless necessary; numeral style rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, omit 'Vol.', 'chap.', and 'p.' in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division, except in reference to ancient/classical authors or works when lower-case Roman numerals should be used; Roman numerals (lower-case) for chapter and pages of introductory matter (Preface, etc.); Arabic numerals for number (No.) and text pages. Use 'Vol.' or 'p.' only when confusion might arise or in exceptional cases; but where the reference is to a page unaccompanied by further details, 'p.' or 'pp.' must of course be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dictates consistent abbreviation and numeral style in bibliographic citations.
